utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. You're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tutnjevic. When we broke for the day yesterday, you said that you had driven Mr. Zaric twice to the communication centre in Bosanski Samac. Please, tell us how you drove Mr. Zaric to the communication centre the first time, and what did you hear and see there?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day I think it was in the early days of the events in Samac, I don't remember the date, Mr. Zaric told me, come on Toso, let's go to the communication centre. Some people from Odzak told me to come to a meeting [as interpreted]. We got into the car outside the command and we went to the communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have some misunderstanding here about what the witness said here on page 1, line 20 -- 21, sorry. "Some people from Odzak told me to come to a meeting." It looks like people from Odzak were waiting for a meeting with Mr. Zaric and this is not actually what the witness said, because we know actually more or less what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can go over that, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: There is a problem, Mr. Tutnjevic, in the interpretation of your words. So please could you just repeat this part that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day, in the early days of the events in Samac, I can't remember the exact date, Mr. Zaric told me, "Come on, Toso, let's go to the communication centre. Some people from Odzak are looking for me. They want me to talk to them about something."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was that in late May, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure, but yes, it was in May, but I'm not sure whether it was late May or another period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zaric perhaps tell you then that some people from the Crisis Staff from Odzak were looking for him?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, from the Crisis Staff in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So did you go with Mr. Zaric to the communication centre?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we got into the car and we went to the communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we reached the communication centre, we found Mr. Kosta Simic, who worked at the centre. With him there was another man, I know his first name was Radovan, he also worked at the centre, and there was another person but I don't remember who.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)we had already arrived when he came, accompanied by two police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we could go into private session perhaps since we are referring to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry, we are not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did the further conversation go between Mr. Zaric and this person who came and said to Mr. Zaric that he was coming from the Crisis Staff meeting of Odzak and what did he say to Mr. Zaric on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing he said was that he had authorisation from the Crisis Staff in Odzak to release some members from Simo's family and to let them go to the other side, to the territory of Bosanski Samac, and he said that Mr. Zaric should dictate the names of these family members of his to him. He had a piece of paper in front of him and he would write them down. Mr. Zaric then raised his voice a bit and said, "Even if my mother, Mileva were there, I would not say that that is my family. My family are all these, I think he said 4.000 persons, and you haven't got enough paper to write down all of their names."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of this person that Mr. Zaric was talking to?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man on the other side of the line also raised his voice when responding to Mr. Zaric. I had the feeling that he was upset because Mr. Zaric spoke to him that way. He said that Mr. Zaric was impudent, that he was rude, and he addressed a few other bad words to him, and he said, finally, that he would come to Samac in a few days and that he would hang Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did Mr. Zaric react to all these insults and threats?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric then reacted by raising his voice, he got up and he said that he would no longer want to speak to him, and he said that nobody should call him there at the communication centre and that is when he ended the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When he said that they should no longer call him for such conversations, is this what he said to Kosta Simic?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He addressed this to Mr. Kosta Simic and the others who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And after that, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, we got into the car and went to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, did you ever drive Mr. Zaric to this centre in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From then, throughout the time while we were together, I never took Mr. Zaric again to this centre. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Since you were with Mr. Zaric very often, do you know whether he ever went to that centre again, this communication centre?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard from anyone that he was driven there, that he went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, you said how you became a driver in the command of the 4th Detachment, and that you drove a passenger vehicle, so tell me now, did you mark this passenger vehicle in any way? Did you put anything on it when you used the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was at the line on the first day, I had a white ribbon on the left-hand side of my blouse. I had it tied to the epaulette of the blouse and I wore this -- I mean in addition to the ribbon, I wore on my own clothing, I had a white ribbon on the antenna of the vehicle but they weren't always white, the colours changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there other signs like this on other vehicles that were used by the army, the civilian Defence, other public institutions?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had yet another vehicle at the command of the 4th Battalion and it had this same kind of white ribbon. I also noticed on other vehicles, I mean even civilians would take these white ribbons and tie them on their upper arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said 4th Battalion. That's what it says here. Is that what you meant or what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned now that civilians wore these white ribbons, which civilians wore that? What was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was worn by civilians of all ethnic backgrounds. It wasn't that anybody ordered that, they did it at their own initiative, most probably for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. I move to strike that last portion of the statement. It's speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be struck off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this other vehicle. When did the command of the 4th Detachment obtain from the Ministry of Defence, department for Bosanski Samac, this other vehicle for their use?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know the date, but it was about 20 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you can remember, who was the driver of this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The driver of this vehicle was Mladen Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he have some kind of a nickname?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rode was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So who did Mladen Radovic nicknamed Rode drive?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I only drove Mr. Simo Zaric, and he drove the rest, the other members of the command of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything, and if so please tell us how you came to know this, what happened to Simo Zaric at the police station when the war started in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I brought Mr. Zaric to the police station, and he went inside and I remained outside. Soon afterwards, he walked out. I noticed that he was angry. He got into the car and I asked him what happened to you? And he said, "Imagine this kid put a pistol in my mouth." And I said, "Which kid?" And he said, "One of those volunteers who came from Serbia." They called him Vuk. And he put a pistol in his mouth. I did not see this but that's what Mr. Zaric told me in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell him -- did he tell you that they had insulted him, threatened him, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that to me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether somebody came to the command and said to Mr. Zaric that he was supposed to report to the police station?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, Milos, Culap came and told him that he had to report to the police station and that's why we went to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know the last name of this man?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His last name was is Culapovic. He is called Milos Culapovic. But everybody called him by the nickname Culap.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the replacement of commander Antic and what were the reasons for which he resigned his post as commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Mr. Antic, Mr. Radovan Antic, I know that in Obudovac, these volunteers from Serbia maltreated him, hit him. And put him in prison where he spent one night, and then when they released him, Mr. Radovan Antic said that he no longer wanted to be commander of the 4th Detachment, that's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After Radovan Antic, who was appointed commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Mr. Antic, his deputy, Jovo Savic, was appointed commander of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when the Army of Republika Srpska was established?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska was established during the month of May, when the Yugoslav People's Army had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's when the decision was reached to establish the Army of Republika Srpska. The Yugoslav army had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the fact that the members of the Yugoslav People's Army who were born in Serbia and Montenegro on the 19th of May actually did leave the territory of the municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army had to leave the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 19th of May and that is when Mr. Nikolic left Pelagicevo as well as everybody else who was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was there some new organisation now of military units of the Army of Republika Srpska in the territory of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, line 14 -- I'm sorry, page 14, lines that they -- the answer there, "The Yugoslav People's Army had to leave the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 19th of May, and that is when Nikolic left Pelagicevo as well as everyone else who was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army." Does he mean the members in Bosanski Samac that were born in Serbia and Montenegro? Is he talking about all of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I don't believe this witness has the proper training and has done any research to determine whether or not members of the Yugoslav army left throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's not clear what he means by everyone. Does he mean everyone in the Samac area, the area that he's familiar with or is he talking about all of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Because if he is talking about all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he doesn't have the -- there is no factual basis to support his statement. In fact, as the Court knows, the United Nations through the Security Council on two or three occasions demanded them to leave. They did it twice during the summer and again they finally indicated on December 2nd that they finally had left, and that was even questionable because the air force was still there through 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner let the defence put their case as they see it. So the witness can answer and all he has to do is explain whether, as Mr. Weiner said, he means -- he meant the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina or just Bosanski Samac. If he meant the whole Bosnia and Herzegovina, then he must explain the basis of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have understood the objections of my colleague, the Prosecutor, and I understand what he wants to know but my question was precise. I asked the witness what he knew about the departure of the members of the Yugoslav People's Army who had been born in Serbia and Montenegro, about their departure from the municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo, but let me clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You understood what I asked you, didn't you? You are talking about the area of the municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You were not talking about all of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not qualified to talk about matters like that. I meant the area of Pelagicevo and Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are aware of the fact that I asked you whether those were only people who had been born in Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours I think we've got the situation clarified now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which unit of the Army of Republika Srpska was established for the territory of Samac and Pelagicevo municipalities?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade came into being.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, where in Republika Srpska did it have its command?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any new structures or organisational changes in Samac, in the town of Samac, as far as the lower ranking military units were concerned?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment ceased to exist and the 5th Battalion came into existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 5th Battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 5th Battalion, that was Mr. Jovo Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact of who the -- who became the commander when Jovo Savic, who had been the commander up to that point, was replaced?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Jovo Savic, Mladen Radovic, nicknamed Rode, became the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember who was appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Mr. Nikolic left, Colonel Mico Djurdjevic was appointed commander of that brigade. He hailed from the same village as I.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you please just tell us what is the name of that village in which Colonel Mico Djurdjevic had been born and which municipality and which republic is it a part of?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village is called Tisina, the distance between Bosanski Samac and Tisina is two kilometres. It is part of the Bosanski Samac municipality and it is in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long Colonel Mico Djurdjevic remained in the position of the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic did not stay there for a very long time. He did not stay the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade for a long time. He stayed for perhaps seven or eight days but not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the dismissal or removal of Colonel Djurdjevic from his position as commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact day but one day Mr. Zaric told me, "Toso, let's go to the heating plant. I have to go to a session of the Crisis Staff." I drove him to the heating plant. He climbed upstairs into the rooms and I remained downstairs with other soldiers. There were those who worked for the Crisis Staff. And after a while, Simo came, we got into the car, and he said, "Take me to the command." When he got into the car he said a new commander had been appointed. What sort of commander? The commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade because Mr. Djurdjevic had been removed or replaced and I said well, who is the new commander? And he said, Mr. Djordjevic has become commander. One of the police officers who had arrived from Serbia. I don't know -- I no longer remember what his first name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that at the police station in Bosanski Samac, at the TO staff building, in the gym of the elementary school building, and the gym of the secondary school building in Bosanski Samac, there were people being held in detention, non-Serbs? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the elementary school building and the secondary school building about people being held in detention there but Croats only. As far as the TO staff building is concerned, most of the people being held there were Muslims and maybe some Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned this in my conversations with people, with police officers. I did go to the TO building very often, where I saw my neighbours and other citizens of Samac. Muslims mostly lived in the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that you went very often to the TO staff building's yard. Let me ask you, did you go into the rooms where those people were being held?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never entered any of the rooms but I did enter the yard and it was quite a large area outside the TO staff building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain why you went to the TO yard?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I even drove into the yard once. Usually I would go because I had many friends who were there. I would bring medicine to them, food, and cigarettes, and fresh laundry for them to wear, fresh underwear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this once that you drove, as you said, into the TO staff yard? Why did you drive into the yard in a car on that day?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived outside the SUP building. I bought Mr. Zaric there, and then when I got out of the car, I noticed a number of civilians who were hiding behind corners with bags in their hands. Some had food in the bags and some had clothes for a change of clothes. I got sick of this whole thing. I came up to a police officer and I asked him whether I could drive a car into the yard to get it washed. He said that I could. I walked about 50 metres from the building to a small side street and I told one of those women who was holding a bag in her hand, that she should bring the stuff to me and that I would put it in the car. So I drove the car into the yard because the police officer had allowed me to, as there was a fountain in the middle of the yard, I said that I would wash the car. I took pen and paper, I made a list of which bag belonged to whom, some bags contained clothes, some bags contained food, I put it inside and I gave it back to people. I distributed this to people. I brought some medicine for one of them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you only drove into the yard in order to be able to take food and medicine and clothes into the yard?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that precisely was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the names of those people, any of those people, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Azem Gibic, he was a Muslim. He was ill. I think he was epileptic. That's what I'd understood. I used to get the same kind of medicine in Serbia before, and I'd bring the medicine to a young boy who was epileptic. Azem Gibic, Fahro Dubric, Perica Misic, Muradif Coralic, and there were some other persons there now but I can't remember all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We have some problems with the transcript, not all the names were properly entered. So please can you just say them once again slowly?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Azem Gibic, Fahro Dubric, Perica Misic, Muradif Coralic, and there were other people there too but I can't remember all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Tutnjevic, did you also bring food and medicine or fresh underwear to some people at the police station? If so, please tell us their names and how did you manage to do that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I brought things to the police station too, every other day I would bring chief [as interpreted] Zaimbegovic clean sheets, that is clean underwear for a change of clothes. I was very good friends with Esref and I would use every opportunity when Mr. Zaric went to the SUP, I would see the duty officer and ask him to allow me to give these things to Esref, the duty officer would usually bring Esref outside to the hall. I would give him the messages from home and I would give him the things that I'd brought for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You did not go into the rooms at the police station building where those people were being held in detention?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never entered a single room there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, one small correction in the transcript, in on page 20, line 12, it says, "chief Zaimbegovic" which might suggest that he was some sort of police chief or something like that but actually his name is Esref, just that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tutnjevic, until when did you stay in the 4th Detachment, which later became the 5th Battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed with the 5th Battalion until the second half of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, was he with the 4th Detachment and later with the 5th Battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska for the whole of this time?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, throughout the period, with the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, was he ever a member of the police in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric was only a member of the 4th Detachment, nothing else, the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And later a member of the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which were Mr. Zaric's tasks, with the detachment and later the battalion, for the whole of this period?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 4th Detachment, he was assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he have the same tasks with the 5th Battalion later on?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had the same tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you are in Samac for the whole of this time. Mr. Zaric and you, did you have any contacts with the citizens of Bosanski Samac, the non-Serb citizens of Bosanski Samac? If so, please tell us what it was about.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had frequent contacts with non-Serbs. Mostly they were prepared to go to the shelter as soon as the shelling began. Usually in the evening, they would sit around and talk late in the evening as they were sitting next to the door to the shelter, Mr. Zaric and I would usually be invited. We would go and visit them and talk to them for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have referred to the shelling. It was wartime. People were getting killed along the front lines. Were there many burials taking place in Samac in that period?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a number of burials, especially in the early days, sometimes as many as four or five a day and there were days when there was not a single burial taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was the person who most frequently spoke at these burials for those members of the Army of Republika Srpska who had been killed or the soldiers of the 4th Detachment of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Zaric was usually the speaker at these funerals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did Mr. Simo Zaric attend the burials of other citizens, other -- his other fellow citizens of Samac, Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever he could, he attended those funerals, regardless of the fact whether the person being buried was Muslim, Serb or a Croat, just like it was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you went together to these funerals, you know this from personal observation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went together.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Djuro Prgomet's family, a Croat from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a bit about them because they were my neighbours. They lived not far from me. Djuro Prgomet was a relation of Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What kind of relation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Zaric's daughter was married to his son, and we often visited the Prgomet family. He was also ill so we would bring medicine to him. We would bring cigarettes, and sometimes food.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. What do you know about the exchange which took place on the 26th of May, 1992, in the village of Zasavica on the River Bosna between Samac municipality and Odzak municipality? Were you present there? Who else was present?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both Mr. Zaric and I attended this exchange. One day, Mr. Zaric told me, Toso, come on, let's go to Zasavica, there is an exchange taking place. I was told that some of my relatives would be there so I want to meet them. I drove Mr. Zaric there and I was present there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Zasavica, where did you stop? Were there other citizens there or rather civilians in the village?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we reached Zasavica, there was a small road -- track slip that forks off the main road towards the River Bosna that's where we left our car. We got out of the car and there were other people there, mostly people from the Odzak area, because they were expecting that some of their relatives would be there, and there were quite a number of people there. When they brought the Croats for the exchange, they passed us by in groups and they walked all the way down to the river bank of the River Bosna because that's where the exchange was taking place except that no one was allowed to be there. I know that there were representatives of the International Red Cross there, representatives of the Samac Red Cross, and a committee but I'm not sure who were the members of this committee for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So did Mr. Zaric meet any of his relatives, family, friends, there?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Zaric had no authority and no official role to play in this exchange. He met two of his relatives there. We put them in the car and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question is did Mr. Zaric meet any of his relatives. That's not an answer to the question and then he's talking about Zaric's authority and official role after he's just said he doesn't know who the members of the committee were. Before he can make a statement like that, he's got to explain his basis of knowledge and that's also not responsive to the question that was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic? You understand what Mr. Weiner has said?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tutnjevic, the question was whether Mr. Zaric met any members of his family, when this exchange in Zasavica took place?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He met two of his relatives. We put them into the car and we went to Samac, to the Tekstilac building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Why did you go to the Tekstilac building?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where a welcome party had been organised for the people who were coming from the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Zaric participated in any way in the carrying out of exchanges, their preparation, organisation, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he had no participation in exchanges whatsoever, and I know that he never went to any other exchange while he was with me or rather while we were together except for this one in Zasavica that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You mean you never drove him there?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And you said that in the 5th Battalion -- I mean that you were in the 5th Battalion until the end of July, 1992. Where did you go -- where were you assigned to towards the end of July, 1992? And who was it that gave you that assignment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of July, 1992, a military council had been established. Mr. Zaric was also a member of this council and that's when we went to Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: As you say, Mr. Zaric went there and he was a member of this military?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Civilian-military council. What about you?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went together with him and I was Mr. Zaric's driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you were not a member of the civilian-military council, you were just the driver of Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the -- a member of the civilian-military council, but I got a decision in writing from the ministry, from the military, to go there because it was some kind of work obligation of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This decision that you got, was that the decision that was issued to you by the Ministry of Defence, department in Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was signed by Mr. Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was president of this civilian-military council in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The President of the civilian-military council in Odzak was Mr. Savo Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other members of this civilian-military council?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other members of this civilian-military council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you came to Odzak, what did you find in Odzak when you came there for the first time? What was the situation like there?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time we came to Odzak, we found many destroyed houses there, and lots of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you find any civilians?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you came there, did you know that in the territory of the municipality of Odzak there had been a military administration that had been introduced?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that there was a military administration, and we were not allowed to move about without approval from this military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Zaric did in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Odzak, Mr. Zaric carried out duties that had to do with morale, religious and political matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about Odzak, please. We are talking about the civilian-military council. What did he do there? Let's do it this way. We are still in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You were Mr. Zaric's driver?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you drive him to while you were in Odzak and what was it that Mr. Zaric did in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part I took Mr. Zaric to the civilians who lived in local communes and who had come from the exchanges. That was later, when exchanges took place. I took him to Samac, to the command, I took him to Pelagicevo again. I took him to the commissioners in local communes. That was it for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you and Mr. Zaric sleep in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We would go home to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you come to work in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would come in the morning at 7.00. If we went directly to Odzak, but sometimes we would first stop at our command in Samac and then we would go to Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you returned from Odzak, when did you return from Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on when Mr. Zaric would finish his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zaric have any contacts with the security organ in the military administration?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military administration, there was a man in charge of security, his name was Mackic. Mr. Zaric often contacted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zaric have any space of his own for work? If so, where was this work space of his?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric had a table in the hotel restaurant in a little corner there, and that is where he conducted his work for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Zaric most often do at that table?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really go into that. I didn't really go into his work. I know that he mostly wrote things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that there was a department of the civilian police in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Odzak, there was a department of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of it was?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mirko Pavic was police commander in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: A short while ago you mentioned that you drove Mr. Zaric to local communes and that you contacted commissioners there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commissioner for the town of Odzak or rather for the local commune of the town of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the local commune of the town of Odzak, the commissioner was Mr. Dusan Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that citizens from Bosanski Samac came to Odzak to do certain work that was part of their work obligation? Do you know anything about that? If so please tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that citizens from Samac came for their work obligation and I often had contacts with them, and they were involved in different kinds of work, starting from cleaning various premises, all the way up to work in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Zaric the person who decided what these people would do in Odzak in relation to their work obligation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Zaric had nothing to do with that, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's not the one who assigned them to their work duties, nor was he supposed to do any such thing with these workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the time while he was in Odzak, was Mr. Zaric a member of the civilian-military council all the time?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric was a member of the civilian-military council all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So while you toured these local communes, did you perhaps drive Mr. Zaric to his parents' home in Trnjak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very first day we came to Odzak, we went to his native village, to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us what you saw there.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came to Mr. Zaric's house, we found embers only. The house had been burned down, only the two chimneys had remained and the house itself had been burned down. There was a building in the yard which was totally destroyed by a shell, riddled or something. This was the house in the yard outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you go to his sister, Mara's house?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. Oh, I did. I did. She was married to a Croat. One day we went to that house too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. And how much time did you and Mr. Zaric spend in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give the exact date, but we spent about a month in Odzak, perhaps a day or two more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's just be a bit more specific. You were in Odzak until --

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of August, like something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go after you left Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric was then assigned to go to the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade in Pelagicevo and I went with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In order to go with Mr. Zaric to the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska in Pelagicevo, did you get a new decision on your appointment from the Ministry of Defence department in Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got a new decision on my appointment from the Secretariat of Defence in Samac and it was just like my work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. In that Posavina Infantry Brigade, were you for the most part Mr. Simo Zaric's driver?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, I was mostly the driver of Mr. Simo Zaric, but from time to time I would drive another man whose name is Makso but I don't know what his last name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell me, please, if you can remember, what did Mr. Zaric do in the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade? What did he head there and at which position was he?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was assistant commander for morale, religious matters and political matters in the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know about political matters. Did you perhaps mean legal matters?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, legal matters, legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Throughout September, when he took up his position as the head of the -- this body for morale, religious and legal matters, what did he do and where did you drive him to?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often I drove him to the commands of other units. I drove him to the front. I drove him to Samac, to the command of the 5th Battalion. I drove him wherever they said things were happening, on the line or that soldiers were unhappy on the line I would drive him to such places for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have just used an expression, the line crumbling. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means the soldiers rebelled and abandoned the line, refused to hold the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were those risky or dangerous tasks that Mr. Zaric had to perform, going to the front line or those sections of the line where soldiers were unhappy?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those tasks entailed a lot of danger, because wherever there was heavy shelling Mr. Zaric would invariably be sent there. Wherever the line had been broken through, Mr. Zaric would be sent there. Once I asked Mr. Zaric, I told him, they are pushing you forward, they want to destroy you. And I asked him to send me back to Odzak. And I told him, if you're meant to be killed, I don't want to join you. And he said, Toso, you're absolutely right. So he sent me back to Odzak. I got another decision from the Secretariat for National Defence and I went back to Odzak, whereas Mr. Zaric stayed back in Pelagicevo and I do not know what happened to him from that moment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave the 2nd Posavina Brigade to return to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr.?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tutnjevic, my name is Pantelic. I defend Mr. Blagoje Simic. I only have a couple of questions to ask you. Tell me, what is the distance between the command in Pelagicevo and Samac, in terms of kilometres?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two roads from Pelagicevo to Samac. If you take the main road, the distance is 20, 30, about 42 kilometres I'd say. If you take the shortcut, across the local hamlet of Josic, I think that's the name of the hamlet, that's the shortcut you can take, which the distance may be about 26 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How long does it take to go by car from Samac to Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It usually takes about 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What's your personal information in relation to those people who were being held, detained, in the SUP building in the TO building, in the first weeks after the war broke out in Samac? Do you have any personal information as to what the reasons had been for their detention? Were those people suspected of having committed any crimes or anything? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that most of the people being held at the TO building were there because they were of other ethnic backgrounds, people like Izetbegovic, Grga Zubak, and several other people, according to my information, had been detained because they were leaders of the SDA and they were preparing certain actions that were to be taken, and they worked on the division of people along ethnic lines [as interpreted]. That's as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was -- what were those events that happened in Samac, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the events that took place between the 16th and the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The answer was not properly recorded, and they worked on the division of people along ethnic lines. This is on page 33, line 12. The witness said they were arming people on ethnic lines. This is what I heard the witness said. So maybe my colleague would clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did you say a while ago when I asked you about your personal information? You talked about Tihic, Izetbegovic and the rest of them. Why were they detained?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the citizens of Serb nationality, of Serb ethnicity in Samac, there was talk that Tihic and the group including the leaders of the SDA were arming the Muslim population mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was their intention? What was the aim? Why were they arming the Muslim population? If you know, tell us, please, if not, just say so?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Phillip Weiner. I work for the Office of the Prosecutor and I'm going to be asking you some questions. Do you understand that? Okay?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that in the spring of 1992, you served as a driver for the defendant Simo Zaric and you drove him on several occasions, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also noted that there was another driver named Rode who also drove people in the command of the 4th Detachment, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes but not initially, not at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you maintain a log, a diary, or any records of who you drove each day?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So at this time there are no records, there are no notes, as to the dates, times, or the persons who you drove?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you're mainly testifying from your memory, isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So as a result, you can't provide an exact date or an exact time that you drove Simo Zaric on each occasion, such as when you drove him to the communication centre? You can't say I drove him on this particular date at this particular time? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the first time is concerned, I can say that it was about 10.00 in the morning. As far as the second time is concerned, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you can't supply an exact date when each of these things happened, as you just are trying to determine from memory and that's over 11 years ago that this happened, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you armed when you were driving Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what sort of arms or arm were you carrying?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an automatic rifle, with a fold-out butt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will continue at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner? Cross-examination continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning again, sir. Now, you testified that you drove Simo Zaric to the SUP on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that the TO was directly across the street, the Territorial Defence building is directly across the street from the SUP?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the defendant Zaric told you that you went there, that you were going there, to interview prisoners, question prisoners, or he was going there to question prisoners, not you yourself?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he questioned prisoners but I know that he did go to the SUP building. Now, whether he took any statements from those who worked at the SUP or from witnesses, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you're aware that Muslims and Croats were being arrested and being held at the SUP and the TO back in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware that Sulejman Tihic had been arrested and that he was the SDA president.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that Simo had told you that he was speaking or interviewing Sulejman Tihic concerning the distribution of weapons? He told you during his interview was called out and Tihic got beaten up? You testified to that.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that Simo had told me that he had gone to see Stiv, someone had called him to see Stiv and once he came back Sulejman had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So at least you're aware that he had been interviewing Sulejman Tihic, that Simo Zaric had been interviewing Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You're also aware that Sulejman Tihic was the SDA president?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not sure if you're aware but Simo Zaric has given three statements or three interviews to the Office of the Prosecutor in April and June of 1998. And Simo during his statement on April 1st, 1998, indicated that the SDS was involved in illegal arming and distribution of arms to the Serb population. Were you aware of that? That the Serbs were being illegally armed by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I only know that the 4th Detachment had been armed by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you have no reason to doubt Mr. Zaric or call him a liar when he says that the SDS was illegally arming Serbs in the Bosanski Samac area?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt his sincerity. He's a man I trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, since Simo Zaric had interviewed Sulejman Tihic concerning illegal arming, do you know whether Simo Zaric ever interviewed or interrogated Blagoje Simic, the President of the SDS, concerning their illegal arming?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, in April or May, did Simo Zaric ever say to you, "Let's go, Toso, bring me to the Crisis Staff building, we are going to interview -- I'm going to interrogate Blagoje Simic concerning the illegal arming by the SDS"? Did he ever say that to you?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Zaric only told me once to drive him to a meeting of the Crisis Staff. The meeting were Mr. Djurdjevic was replaced but that was the only time I drove Simo to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that very shortly but did Simo ever say we are going to meet Blagoje Simic because I have to interrogate him or interview him concerning the SDS's illegal arming of the Serbs in the municipality of Bosanski Samac? Did he ever say that to you? To drive him to a certain location so he could do that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Zaric never told me that he would interview Mr. Blagoje Simic. He never told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did Simo Zaric tell you that he had or was intending to interview any of the SDS leaders concerning the illegal arming of the SDS -- by the SDS of the local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with the question but maybe Mr. Weiner could be more specific about SDS leader, or who he's referring him, local Serbs, SDS, it doesn't make much sense to me, whether he means in what level, who these men were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll withdraw the question and rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric ever tell you that he had interviewed any municipal SDS members from the Bosanski Samac municipality concerning their illegal arming of the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Zaric never told me that he had talked about anything to the representatives of the SDS. I know that there was a bit of ill feeling between them because Mr. Zaric was a member of a different party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But he never told you that he had interviewed any SDS members, any municipal SDS members of Bosanski Samac, concerning illegal distribution of weapons?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never told me anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you know who Blagoje Simic is?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Blagoje Simic is a doctor from Bosanski Samac. He is also my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that in 1992 he was the SDS president?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were also aware that he was the Crisis Staff president in 1992, in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of who the President of the Crisis Staff was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, sir, in the spring of 1992, April, May and June, did you see Blagoje Simic? Did you ever happen to see him as you were driving Simo Zaric around? Did you see him in the Bosanski Samac area?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see Blagoje Simic about town, like many other people. I would meet him in the street sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet him in the area of the police station, TO, or municipal building that area where all three buildings are located? Or did you ever see him in that area?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Mr. Blagoje Simic in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While you were driving Simo Zaric, did you ever see him around town?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I went with Simo I never saw him in town. It was only my free time when I went on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, sir, you indicated that you drove Simo to the communication centre so he could speak with officials from Odzak, and you did that twice in the month of May, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I drove Mr. Zaric to the communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were present on the first occasion or were you present on the first occasion for all of the discussions which occurred over the radio? For the entire conversation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for the entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you recall -- do you recall, sir, Simo Zaric telling those persons or officials from Odzak that he would consult with members of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac about their proposals for exchanges? Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did say that he would consult with those members, that he would inform the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And without saying names of the other person who was involved in the conversation, you recall that there were -- there was discussion about an all-for-all for a flock-for-flock exchange? Do you recall that? Without saying the name of the other person who was involved.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after that conversation, where did you bring Simo next?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that conversation, we went to the command of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you -- a few days later you again returned to the communication centre, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you drove Simo to the communication centre on that -- about two or three days later, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And on the way, did he tell you that he had advised the Crisis Staff about the nature and contents of his initial conversation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not tell me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. For the second time we have this expression, advised the Crisis Staff. I would prefer if the correct word would be informed the Crisis Staff, because this is what figures in Mr. Zaric's interview. Maybe I don't need to go through this again but this was the objection that I already made, because in our language, there is a very significant difference and what we hear as translation was that Mr. Zaric was -- shows Mr. Zaric had some sort of adviser in respect to this topic, and the other issue is if he just informed the Crisis Staff. So if we are quoting Mr. Zaric's interview, the proper word would be "informed."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour I have no problem with that. As the Court knows in English the term advise means either to counsel or to inform. So I'm not trying to misrepresent what happened but I'd be happy to use the word inform. It makes no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you present for the entire radio conversation on the second occasion too?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, just before I --

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just be allowed to add, I was present while Simo was having an argument with a man from Odzak, the second conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before that, again Simo Zaric has given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor where he indicates that he informed the Crisis Staff president, Stevan Todorovic, and other Crisis Staff members, about an all-for-all exchange and that they were not opposed to this type of exchange. Did Simo Zaric ever tell you of that? Whether it's either on the ride to -- you said he didn't tell you about that on the ride to the communication centre. Did he tell you about that at any other time?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understood your question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Simo Zaric states, after the first conversation, he did meet with some Crisis Staff members, the President of the Crisis Staff, Stevan Todorovic, and certain Crisis Staff -- and certain other Crisis Staff members. He states that in his statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on April 2nd, 1998, at page 80. And that's P141 ter. Did Simo Zaric ever tell you about this meeting with the Crisis Staff and its members, where he told them about an all-for-all exchange and they were not opposed to such an exchange? Did Simo Zaric ever tell you about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Zaric never told me anything about his contacts with the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you attend the second -- the second radio communication session. Were you present for the entire conversation where all the different parties spoke? Without saying the names of the parties. Were you present for all of those conversations?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there in those rooms while Mr. Zaric was having an argument with them. Later I came out into the hall and the door was ajar so I could overhear the conversation of that other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you weren't present for the entire conversation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you present, sir, when Simo Zaric told the Odzak officials that the crisis -- that he had advised the Crisis Staff about the all-for-all proposal, an all-for-all exchange, and that they did not object to it? Were you present for that portion of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't. I was present when Simo Zaric talked about the two relatives of that gentleman from Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Simo Zaric's statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that he advised the Odzak officials about the Crisis Staff's view that they would not oppose an all-for-all exchange of persons between Samac and Odzak, do you have any reason to disbelieve that statement?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he said that, I have every confidence in him. He is a man I trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talked about being a driver for Simo Zaric and for others, for many years, about 30 years you served as a driver, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, throughout your career, not just working for the municipality but also prior to working for the army and your whole career was as a driver, as opposed to your training as an auto mechanic?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never worked as a driver for Simo Zaric until I came to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I know that. Prior to joining the 4th Detachment in 1992, you had been a driver for a number of years, not for Simo Zaric but a driver?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And during this long career as a driver, did you pass throughout the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a driver, I lived in Bosanski Samac. I resided in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also drove throughout the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... with the villages and settlements and hamlets within Bosanski Samac having driven through for many years?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated you're from the village of Tisina?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was born in the village of Tisina, and I live in Bosanski Samac. I have been living there since 1960, and I live at the following address, the street of Car Dusan number 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, and you're familiar that south of the town of Bosanski Samac and south of the village of Tisina are the villages or settlements of Donji Hasici and Gornji Hasici, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the south of the village of Tisina is Hrvatska Tisina, Donji Hasic, Gornji Hasic and the village of Skaric [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're familiar with those two villages of Donji Hasici and Gornji Hasici?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And those two villages are mainly or were mainly populated by Croats in the early 1990s, prior to April 17th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Croats lived in these two villages. In Donji Hasic, there are only two or three ethnic Serb families.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're also aware that in 1994, these two villages were combined and a new single village was established called Srnice?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, it is beyond the time frame of the indictment. We all know that for the two co-accused here, the time frame is up to December, 1993, and for the other is the end -- the third one is the end of 1992, so it's well beyond the time frame of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: First it's a historical fact that these two villages were combined into one. Number 2, in Exhibit P126, Blagoje Simic signs the order from the assembly of Bosanski Samac or the assembly of Samac combining these two villages and why this is relevant is earlier in this case, we prevented certain types of cross-examination indicating or we objected to certain types of cross-examination indicating that these two villages were separate and distinct. Counsel or Defence indicated they were one single village. We have a copy of the order showing that they were in fact two separate settlements of villages, that they were combined in 1994, and it's also -- it's informative for the Court to know that they were in fact two separate villages and it relates to our objection because we objected to certain testimony basically documents from one village being reviewed by a witness who lived in another village on the basis that they were in fact two separate villages. In fact Judge Lindholm displayed his map and showed that they were two -- that he believed that they were two separate villages. Counsel indicated he was going to offer proof at some later time that they were in fact one village -- it was in fact one village. When witnesses were questioned thereafter they all indicated it was two separate villages and since this man is a driver, has been a driver for many years, has driven throughout the municipality, I'd like to introduce through him the fact that these were -- that these were in fact two separate villages just as our witnesses said, just as the testimony before the Court, and just as this document which is signed by this defendant right here, indicates that they were two separate villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may add, please, we have discussion about the -- these two villages which according to the position of the Defence were in fact one settlement, and that's a matter for the other experts, not for this person here. Number 2, it is not true what my learned friend just said, that Mr. Blagoje Simic signed this decision. Actually, it was not a decision, it was a conclusion, and on behalf of the assembly of -- municipal assembly of Samac in capacity of a chairman of assembly, a speaker of assembly, he was obliged to sign that -- this conclusion. And finally, Your Honour, this is not a matter here to discuss with a person who can testify only on facts. So maybe the question could be limited or rephrased whether this person, this witness, is aware of the, I would say, conditions or, I don't know, kind of territorial issues regarding these two villages. That might be question. But to introduce to this witness a paper which is beyond the time frame of the indictment, that's the basis for the objection of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document is already in evidence in this Court in P126 ter. I want to introduce the English portion of that section. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that the Prosecution will be allowed to put the questions to this witness, as he was familiar with the region. Notwithstanding the fact that the decision was in 1994, it is so connected to the verification of the fact whether or not the two villages were separate, and as this is a contentious matter between the two parties, I think it's just fair that the Prosecution should be allowed to put the exhibit to the witness so that he can explain. Not explain the decision because he's not the one who made it but discuss the matter as the Prosecution want to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question again to you was: Were you aware that the two villages of Gornji Hasici and Donji Hasici were combined and became the village of "Srnic"?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gornji Hasic and Donji Hasic was later called not "Srnic" but the village of Srnice. That's the proper name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they were combined together and called Srnice?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called the village of Srnice because ethnic Serbs moved there from the municipality of Gradacac. They were expelled from a village there called Srnice. So then they called themselves Srnice here. Now, I don't know whether they themselves started calling themselves Srnice or whether there was a decision that ruled on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness some documents and also introduce them into the Court. Could the usher assist us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the record this is page 30 of P126 ter, and the ERN number at the top is 00456676.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to invite your attention to decision number 62. Do you see the 62 on the left? On the left column, sir? Sir, why don't I read it and could you look along as I read it? I'll read it and could you follow along, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
