utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could a copy be placed on the ELMO for our clients?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure that could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What I'm going to read to you, I'm going to read the English translation to you. Can you follow along with me, can you follow along with me, please? Do you see where it says, at the top, "Pursuant to Article 50 of the Statute of Samac municipality, municipal assembly of Samac"? Do you see that, sir? "In its session held on 11 March, 1994, brought the decision on the joining of settlements and changing of the name of a settled place." Municipal -- okay then there is a one, roman numeral 1: "Municipal assembly of Samac, considering an initiative from settlements Gornji Hasic and Donji Hasic and Prud, considers as necessary to A, join settlements of Gornji Hasic and Donji Hasic into one settlement that would be called Srnice." Is that correct, my reading of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then it says, "Change the name of Prud settlement into a new name, Njegosevo." Did I pronounce that correctly?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Roman numeral 2: "The act of joining of settlements and changing the name of a settlement referred to in the last paragraph herein will be carried out by government or people's assembly of RS, in accordance with the law." Did I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Roman numeral 3: "The decision is to be released in the Official Gazette of RS." And there is a date to the left of March 15th, 1994, and to the right, president of the municipal assembly, Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'd like to move the introduction of this document, the English has been done by our translation unit. We are awaiting an official translation from the Tribunal so I'd like to move this at least as an ID document at this time. The English portion of it, although P126 has already been -- P126 ter has already been admitted, there is also another section that was later introduced which would be P126A and A ter so this we would request be P126A for ID, I'm sorry, P126B for ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, objection to the admission, since it was never admitted as my learned friend stated, we didn't object to the admission, if you see just on this page, on the ELMO, it's very visible, all other -- all other decisions on that page are from 1993, except that one. So in Pre-Trial proceedings and during the admission of this particular Official Gazette, which was published in 1994, but consisted of various decisions from 1993, which is within the scope of the -- temporal scope of the indictment, we didn't object. Now on the back door, my learned friend tried to introduce this decision, which is by the way is nonsense, it is not a decision, it is conclusion, so that's a first objection to the translation, then in paragraph 3, it is stated that it will be published in Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, what is the relation between municipal assembly and Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, et cetera. But the basic objection Your Honour is that it is beyond the temporal scope of the indictment and finally it was actually admitted only partially this Official Gazette was admitted only partially related to the decisions issued and adopted in 1993, which is the -- which is the case here, and by chance, or I don't know by which procedure, this conclusion was printed in this particular Official Gazette, and obviously, it's beyond the year 1993. That is the basis of objection of the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I assist the Trial Chamber with yet another fact? If it is truly the intention of the Prosecution to prove what they said a short while ago, I think that in relation to these facts, it is relevant to note the demographic analysis of Mrs. Ewa Tabeau that has already been tendered. These two villages are mentioned as two villages. And this will also be mentioned in our expert's opinion on this subject. So I think this is relevant in relation to what the Prosecution is trying to prove. Of course, if the Prosecution is trying to prove something different, then I support what my colleague just said. This is beyond the scope of the indictment, and then it is really not relevant to what the Prosecutor said that he is trying to show us, namely that there are two settlements. So how can this be proven?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no limitation indicated in the records from the Registry or that I'm aware of when 126 ter was introduced, so this document is technically before the Court. I'm just introducing the English version of one of the sections. Since it is already in evidence, we could refer to this any ways, because it is an exhibit before the Court. However, offering the English version and it is basically being offered to provide proper information to the Court, which is consistent with the testimony from the witnesses, that these were two separate villages, and that's all we are looking to do. Counsel indicated that they were one village, without any proof. He indicated he was going to bring some expert testimony, which they never did. And his own client, the defendant Blagoje Simic, was the President of the municipal assembly when this decision was passed, and I'm just offering it, the English version, as an ID document, which does nothing more than shows the Court what exactly the facts were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber will allow the exhibit. It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This decision will be treated as document P126B ID. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified that sometime, I'm assuming in late 1991, early 1992, you received a call-up notice from the Ministry of Defence. Was that early 1992?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, I think, it was in January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you were not ordered to report to the local TO. Rather, you were ordered to report to the SIT building, which was the -- you were ordered to report to the 4th Detachment, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called up by the Secretariat of National Defence and I responded to this call-up, and therefore came to the building of the Secretariat for National Defence, that is where I was informed that I was assigned to the 4th Detachment and its seat, its headquarters, was in the SIT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you weren't ordered to report to the local TO, rather you were told to report to the 4th Detachment, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called up to report at the Secretariat for National Defence and I was told there that I was assigned to the 4th Detachment, and that I should report at the SIT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. They did not tell to you report to the local TO, Territorial Defence, that's all I'm trying to -- they did not tell to you report to the local Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, as you know, the 4th Detachment was a unit of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you received -- you had certain positions within that JNA unit. You were a platoon commander and then you were eventually the command driver?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a platoon commander. I was commander of a squad for one day only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were a squad commander and then you were or eventually you were named as the driver, okay.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in May, you testified that the JNA had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army of the Republika Srpska was established?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you testified that the 4th Detachment becomes -- the 4th Detachment of the JNA's 17th Tactical Group becomes a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Yugoslav People's Army left, the Army of Republika Srpska was established, and the 4th Detachment became a military formation of the Army of Republika Srpska, or rather at that time the name of the 4th Detachment was changed, or rather instead of the 17th Tactical Group, there was the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade and the 5th Battalion of that brigade was the former 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So basically one day you were a member of the JNA 4th Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group and then you're suddenly a member of the 5th Battalion of the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a driver in the command of the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you went from the JNA, being a member of the JNA, to being a member of the Army of the Republika Srpska, you and the other members of the 4th Detachment went from being the 4th Detachment of the JNA to being the 5th Battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to show you a statement from the Tadic judgement. You're aware that several judgements have been issued by this Court, not Miroslav Tadic, but you're aware that this Court --

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- I saw it on television, that this Court passed a few judgements but I don't know about Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to show you a portion of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, maybe just to can clear this up, because the witness just said I don't know about Miroslav Tadic, maybe we should say Dusan Tadic and get it clear that we are talking about somebody completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm going to show you is the Dusan Tadic, known as Dule Tadic, judgement, and I just want to show you two paragraphs in that concerning the transfer of the JNA units to the VRS or the Army of Republika Srpska units, and I'd like to go over them with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you hold on, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there would be any ruling about this but I would like to ask my friend, colleague, my learned colleague what is the relevance of showing to this witness, factual witness, a driver in the small detachment, and ask him to make any comment about the judgement of this Tribunal. I really don't see it's appropriate witness for this kind of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: First of all, before we -- the Trial Chamber makes any ruling we would like to find out what you intend to do with the passages of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have passages of the judgement and I want to show it to him and they can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, it's the Trial Chamber. And they concern the transfer of the units from the JNA to the VRS, from the JNA units to the Army of Republika Srpska unit and ask him isn't that the exact same thing that happened in Bosanski Samac? As he just testified he was a JNA member one day, in the 4th Detachment, and the next day, he's a 5th Battalion member in the VRS: I have copies, if the Court would like to see the two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. The point is those are the findings of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, and those weren't issues that were appealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That doesn't matter. That doesn't matter. This witness has testified about what happened or what -- how the various army units were moved around or transferred or renamed and he should be cross-examined on the facts according to his evidence. I don't think it's proper to put a finding -- a judgement to this particular witness. That is a matter for submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll just ask him further questions about the transfer, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you went from the 4th Detachment of the JNA to becoming a member of the 5th Battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska, in transferring from one army to another, you didn't have to return your rifle? You were allowed to keep your rifle, isn't that correct? The rifle that was issued to you by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have to return my rifle. I carried it around with me until the 1st of October, 1993, when I left the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated that the JNA gave you what was known as a RAP. It was like gun-cleaning equipment and ammunition. You didn't have to return that when you left the JNA and became a member of the VRS, Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have to return it because that was part of the equipment used with the automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your uniform that you received when you became a member of the 4th Detachment, that JNA uniform, did you have to return that when you left the JNA and were transferred to the VRS or the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got my first uniform from the JNA. It was SMB or rather olive-drab. That's the standard Yugoslav equipment. Later on, this was replaced with a camouflage uniform and that uniform I could not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did you receive the camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camouflage uniform, I received it -- I don't remember the date but I think it was in late July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But up to the point where you received the camouflage uniform, were you still wearing the JNA uniform that you had been issued when you joined the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you went from being a member of the JNA to being a member of the Army of Republika Srpska, were you given any choice as to whether or not to accept this transfer, from one army to another?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers were not given any choice as to which unit they would belong to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, sir, let's move on. In July, you were -- you were sent to Odzak. Now, --

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, you followed Simo Zaric to Odzak. Simo Zaric was assigned to the civilian-military council by the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. I believe that we already have the testimony of this witness that he was sent there by the Ministry of Defence in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, Simo Zaric, not this witness, Simo Zaric is the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you limit it whether he has any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question was Simo Zaric was assigned to the civilian-military council by the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who appointed the members of the military council but I do know that Simo told me one day, "Tomorrow we are going to Odzak." Several days later I received a decision in writing from the military ministry in Samac that my assignment would be in Odzak. That was my military, wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you and Simo -- you and the defendant --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't want to interrupt but here we have using of some words that have quite a different meaning. Wartime assignment is a completely different. He said it was my work obligation. These are the exact words that the witness used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps Mr. Weiner can ask him to describe what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were assigned -- you, not Simo Zaric, you were assigned to Odzak by whom?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who assigned me but Simo Zaric told me that we would go to Odzak. And then several days later I got a decision in writing from the military ministry, ministry of the army of the Serbian Municipality of Samac, that my work obligation would be with the civilian-military council in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, were you aware that Simo Zaric in Odzak was serving as the deputy to the President of the war council for security matters? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again, according to what we know and what we hear as the translation, there is again one word that we have a problem with this. Not deputy but assistant. And it makes a significant difference. I believe that we already explained the difference between deputy and assistant within the 4th Detachment and it does make a difference because the deputy is the person who in the absence of the president replaces him, and takes all his duty, while assistant has a very different position. He's the one who assists for certain topics. So what we have is that Mr. Zaric was assistant of the President, not the deputy of the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm reading from the joint statement of admissions by the parties, matters which are not in dispute and that's on page 13 where it says deputy to the president, but I'll agree with counsel, I'll use the word assistant to the President. It makes no difference to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that Simo Zaric served as the assistant to the President of the war council for security matters?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that Simo Zaric was the assistant of the President of the military council, but not of the War Presidency. He was in charge of morale, religious and legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not indicating that he was a member of the War Presidency. He was the assistant to the President and was he not involved in intelligence and security matters while he was in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated, or you testified earlier today that you really -- you testified earlier today that you really didn't go into his work or you really didn't know about his work but you mostly saw him write things down. You testified about that on pages 27 and 28 today. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you weren't examining his writings?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you weren't reading or reviewing what he was writing down, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So since you never examined what he was writing down, you can't state or you don't know if what he was writing down concerned the assignment of labourers, because you had never read those documents that he was drafting.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, he told me that he had nothing to do with the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question concerned labour assignments but since you were not reading any of those documents that he was drafting, you don't know or you can't state if his documents concerned projects needing labour or the number of labourers needed to complete projects. You can't state that because you never read those documents, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Since you never reviewed any of the documents that Mr. Zaric wrote, you don't know if they concerned the labourers that were coming from Samac? You never read them so you can't say what they concerned.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he never requested workers to be placed under his work obligation. I know because all the commissioners, all the companies had their own commissioners and these commissioners requested workers for the next day to be brought over from Samac. I know that Simo Zaric never made any such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, since you never reviewed or read any documents that he had written, you don't know whether or not they concerned labour, because you never read them. You can't say, you never read those documents, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine. I didn't read them, but I knew from our mutual communication, from our talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But since you never read those documents, you can't be sure that they didn't concern labour assignments, you never read them.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he would have told me if he had requested workers, and probably he would have known where to send them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is not your discussions with him. Since you never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, we spent so much. The witness has given you the answers he can give. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree with me that after April 17th, life in Samac had changed drastically?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There had been an elected government in 1990 that was no longer in office.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A Serb Crisis Staff had taken over the government in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The SDA president, Sulejman Tihic, and its vice-president, Izet Izetbegovic, were in jail?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that Blagoje Simic was the President of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you, sir, were not a member of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you weren't a member because you didn't agree with their policies or politics?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, you're aware that Biljana Plavsic, the former SDS and Bosnian Serb leader has pled guilty in this Court to orchestrating a campaign of persecution against the non-Serb population of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as part of her plea, she has admitted to a SDS policy of the permanent removal of ethnic populations, the non-Serb ethnic populations, from Serbian territory. You as a Yugoslav, you weren't in favour of that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understood the question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Biljana Plavsic admitted to a SDS policy of the permanent removal of the non-Serb population from territory controlled by the Serbs. You, as a Yugoslav, was not in favour of those deportations and expulsions.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was certainly not in favour of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, she also admits, in paragraph 19, that the SDS and Serb leadership implemented a persecution campaign by various means. One of those means was the unlawful detention and killing of non-Serbs. As a Yugoslav, you weren't in favour of that policy of unlawful killing and detention of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at this situation in Samac, you didn't like what happened in Crkvina, where 16 non-Serb men were killed? You didn't like that. You were appalled by that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't like it. Most of the citizens of Bosanski Samac didn't like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you didn't like the killing of Dikan, which you learned about, which occurred on or about April 26, 1992, at the Territorial Defence building? You didn't like that.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were also aware, as you've testified, that many non-Serbs in Samac were being arrested and isolated.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that many of these arrests were based on nothing other than their ethnicity, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you being a Yugoslav did not like that either.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And Biljana Plavsic, also in that paragraph 19 of the factual basis supporting her plea, talks about the use of cruel and inhumane treatment, and inhumane conditions in detention facilities. That's what she admits that she and the SDS and the Bosnian Serb leaders used, cruel and inhumane treatment, and inhumane conditions in detention facilities. You, sir, as a Yugoslav, you didn't like that.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I don't like politics. I think it's below me to discuss such issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, we have to discuss it for the Court, so let me just ask you a few questions and we'll move on. But you as a Yugoslav, you didn't like that SDS and Serb policy of cruel and inhumane treatment and inhumane conditions in the detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, this witness just ten seconds before said that he was not aware of that, and my learned friend is trying to put same question to him. So maybe it could be rephrased or maybe he can leave this topic and go to another topic because we have that in transcript, it's page 64, line 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour my question is whether or not he agrees with the policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And he was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He can say does he agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's the same question. You didn't like that and then you didn't like the SDS and so forth --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll ask him --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The SDS and Bosnian Serb policy of the use of cruel and inhumane treatment and inhumane conditions in detention facilities, you do not agree with that policy?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you've testified you visited several friends at the various prison camps, the TO, the SUP, the primary school, the high school, you had many friends at those camps.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only visited my friends at the TO, in the yard of the TO, and at the SUP building. I never went to the elementary or secondary school buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. You knew people were being held at the elementary and secondary school buildings?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that these were non-Serbs, Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you had good friends at the SUP being held at the police station, and the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said one of them was "Esrem" Zaimbegovic?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, his name was Esref, Esref Zaimbegovic, not "Esrem." Yes. He's the one I went to see most often.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was a good friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He wasn't a criminal of any kind?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a criminal of any kind. He wasn't into politics. He was a businessman, a good one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was being held because of his ethnicity, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, while you were went to see these -- while you went to see these friends, and as you also spoke to others who visited friends and relatives, you learned that the conditions at these places were not very good, at the TO and the SUP?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware that these were inhumane conditions, that people were being beaten, mistreated?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware that there was poor hygiene?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware that there was little food?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the kind of food they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you knew that families were sending food in or trying to get food in?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know about that, and many times I brought food to a number of people. But Mr. Zaric knew this too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And which, when you said Mr. Zaric was aware of this too, do you mean the poor treatment of the prisoners or do you mean that you were bringing food, or both?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant whether I was bringing food to these prisoners myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that was actually very kind of you to bring the food to them. And sir, these poor conditions that you saw in Bosanski Samac, that's consistent with Biljana Plavsic's statement of inhumane conditions in detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you agree that the conditions were poor in Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated, just as we are finishing this, that certain people were isolated in Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the persons that were isolated were the non-Serbs, the Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And by being isolated, it means that they were being detained, not for committing crimes but because of their ethnicity, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object to this question. I mean, this is a bit of legal matter. Isolated, it's one question. And being detained, it's maybe another question. Because in our language, there are -- there is no difference between being detained or in isolation, and it is usually related to some procedures against some person so asking this witness whether it was because of their ethnicity or something like that, it's a call for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think so. We've had a lot of testimony in this case about isolation from both Prosecution witnesses and Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think in fairness to the witness, it's better to brake down your question and also ask him whether he knows of any reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that certain people, certain non-Serbs, I'm sorry, that the non-Serbs of Bosanski Samac were being isolated.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were they being isolated?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were isolated in the village of Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were these men, women, children, elderly? What were they?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were women there, and children, and elderly people, and there were entire households that were put up in individual houses in Zasavica and they led a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And these people that were isolated in Zasavica, it was -- you said women, children and elderly. Where were the husbands?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The older husbands were there in isolation in Zasavica and others, some of them, were in the TO building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these women, these children, these elderly people, were they isolated because they had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They were isolated in Zasavica because of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when we talk about isolation of people in Zasavica and elsewhere, we are not talking about a handful of people, we are talking about over 100 people?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go to Zasavica. I don't know how many of them there were there but I just heard that there were people in Zasavica who were in isolation, and there was a considerable number in Samac as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say there was a considerable number in Samac, between Samac and Zasavica, we are talking about a large number of people?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the reason those people in Samac were isolated was because of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those who were isolated probably, yes, but there were some people who were not in isolation at all. There were people who lived in their houses, their own houses, and they went out for work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these people in Samac that were isolated, those were non-Serbs, those were Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified that -- about the isolations in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P141 ter, please? Page 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to read that to you and have you follow along with me. Would you please do that? On the bottom of page 72, in the B/C/S, I'll read the top part, Zaric: "It is a Croatian village, and a number, as far as I know, inhabitants remained after the outbreak of the conflict. Before the conflict, some left, presumably to go to Croatia and to other villages in the area. The Samac Crisis Staff had decided at some point -- sorry, at some point, I know that, I don't know when the decision was made, on the isolation of Croats, and they were then, a number of them, were taken from Samac and put in these -- placed in these abandoned houses in Zasavica, or also were made to -- for them, accommodation to be provided by those people already living there."

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Why don't you read --

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not what it says here on this page, on this sheet of paper. There is a different text here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why don't you read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe, maybe I understand and again we have the same problem because you are reading it in English, we have a simultaneous translation and it is not always the same one as it is written in the statement. So maybe to assist the interpreters this should be put on the ELMO so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you put it on the -- could you put it and just if you could turn slightly? And you can follow along. Or you can watch it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it better this way. I can see it better this way. Oh, oh, I see, right, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can the translators see it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, why don't we take our break now and I'll make a copy for the translators so we can get through this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour apparently the problem was according to translation. There is a difference between the page numbers between the exhibit and what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well then, show the witness the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They are saying it's 76 but...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Appears to be 72 and 73 in my copy as well as the copy that the witness has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What matters is to read the corresponding paragraph, isn't it? Not necessarily the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm doing. I'm reading it in -- I'll read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Page 72, middle of the page, Zaric answer: "It is a Croatian village and a number, as far as I know, inhabitants remained after the outbreak of the conflict. Before the conflict some left, presumably to go to Croatia or to other villages in the area. The Samac Crisis Staff had decided at some point, I know that, I don't know when the decision was made, on the isolation of Croats and they were then... a number of them were taken from Samac and put in these, placed in these abandoned houses in Zasavica or also were made to... for them, accommodation to be provided by those people already living there. I don't think it was a camp in a typical sense because they were able to walk about, but certainly, I know about the decision and this was one very unfortunate, very bad decision made by the Crisis Staff." Question: "So this was the Crisis Staff in Samac at some point decided that the Croats living in Samac municipality should be removed from their homes and sent to Zasavica?" Answer, Zaric: "This was not exclusively for Croats because there were also some Muslim families there, I believe. The decision was made following the imprisonment of those people in the Odzak area. I think it wasn't just for the Croats." Were you able to follow along, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the same like your text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you read what's different?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I think that it wasn't only Croats who were there. They also took some Muslim families there. So this decision on isolation, this isolation, later pertained to part of the Muslims too. There were some Muslim families there, as far as I know, and this decision on isolation was adopted after Serbs were taken prisoner in the area of Novi Grad, as far as I know people had to leave their homes and go to Zasavica."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when they say it was done in your words or in your reading, it was done after the Serbs were taken prisoner in Novi Grad, Novi Grad is in Odzak, in the Odzak municipality, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these facts which Simo Zaric gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, are you aware of these?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you're aware of the Crisis Staff's decision to isolate the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know whose decision that was. I just know that the non-Serb population was taken into isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- are you aware of any reason why Simo Zaric would say it was the Crisis Staff's decision to isolate the non-Serb population if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not doubt the truthfulness of what Simo Zaric says at all, but I had no knowledge of that being the decision of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, how long have you known Simo Zaric, sir?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known Simo Zaric well for over 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's why he was comfortable in having you as his driver? You know each other for a long time, you trust each other?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he chose me in particular but he trusted me. We knew each other and we socialised before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, trusting each other, because you trusted each other, you were able to talk to each other while you were in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you told him, as you've testified, that you were delivering food to the prisoners, food, medical supplies, clothing?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he also told you about certain things, he told you about the beatings, the mistreatment and the killings of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me about the mistreatment of prisoners and he told me about a killing that had happened, and I had never heard about that from anyone. It's only from Simo Zaric I heard about that from. And that was Dikan's murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you both discussed the poor conditions in these prison camps or detention centres? He told you about the mistreatment and you told him about what you had seen?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about everything, but what I knew could not have been known by each and every soldier and each and every citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But when you say you talked about everything, both of you talked about the poor conditions at those detention centres? You conversed at times about that? Your knowledge, his knowledge, and you talked about it?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also talked about what was happening, what the police were doing? Did Simo tell you about what Todorovic was doing and what the police were doing and some their actions, or the improper actions if you want to call them, mistreatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only Simo who told me about that. He did not tell me about what Todorovic did. This could have been heard from other policemen, that there were mistreatments, and one evening, Simo picked up these prisoners and drove them to Brcko so that they would not be mistreated and abused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. But so you knew about Todorovic and Simo knew about Todorovic and it was kind of common knowledge as to what was happening?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was common knowledge, it was no secret, ordinary citizens of Bosanski Samac knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just like Crkvina, people knew about Crkvina too, the terrible killing of those 16 people?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric and I went to Pelagicevo the next day. When we returned to Samac, many inhabitants had already known about what had happened in Crkvina that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So let's get this straight. You knew about -- both you and Simo knew about the isolation of the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The mistreatment of the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The unlawful arrest of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The brutal actions of the volunteers from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The mistreatment of prisoners by the police? The mistreatment of the non-Serb prisoners by the police.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the killing of certain non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So at some point, you and Simo are aware of this system of persecution of the non-Serbs of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is calling for legal conclusion from this witness. He knew about all these acts but whether these were -- it was a system of persecution, this is not that simple to ask a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But it's obvious in the spring of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, because all these things have been discussed before, even with this witness, several times, I don't see why you should continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm just getting into the area of knowledge, as to who knew about what, that's all, and I'm just finishing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But all of these things were happening in the spring of 1992, to the non-Serb civilians in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, sir, you talked about being a driver for Simo Zaric in several places and in several units, and at various times. Now, you said that Simo Zaric had told you at sometime you were both going to Odzak and shortly there after, the Ministry of Defence assigns you to Odzak where you then serve as Simo Zaric's driver, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Simo Zaric had you transferred or initiated the transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. It's calling for speculation. The witness clearly answered that he received a decision of the ministry. Whether Simo Zaric were they both transfer, who issued orders or whatever, this is not up to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think we should look at the witness's knowledge. Does he know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, did Simo Zaric have you transferred?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that I got a decision from the Ministry of National Defence that I should go to Odzak as a driver at that military council there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At sometime, Simo Zaric leaves Odzak and he goes to the 2nd Posavina command in Pelagicevo, and you thereafter go with him?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Again to be his driver?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And prior to being transferred, did he tell you that you were going to be going with him to the 2nd Posavina command?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not tell me. He just said to me one day, Toso, tomorrow we are going to Pelagicevo and we are going to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And after he says that, the Ministry of Defence notifies you that you've been transferred to Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then after being in Pelagicevo, you didn't like it there, or you didn't like going to the front lines with Simo there, you thought it was dangerous?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You wanted to return to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I did return.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But Simo told you you could go back to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Simo talked to people at the Secretariat for National Defence and then I got a decision once again that I was going back to Odzak and that this was my work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you got transferred after Simo spoke to the people at the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, you indicated you didn't like being on the front line. Where was the front line?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This front line was in the area of Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was on the other side? Who were you facing? What troops? Soldiers from what troops? I'm sorry, soldiers from where? What armies? HVO? HV?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I just know that there are Croat villages there and probably there are soldiers too but we did have information that there were soldiers there from the Republic of Croatia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any questions from other counsel before re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tutnjevic, tell me, now when you told the Prosecutor about your work obligation, Odzak, and then about the going to Pelagicevo and so on, you were a soldier of the Army of Republika Srpska then, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a soldier and then after that, I got decisions as a work obligation, and the first decision about work obligation, I got when I set out to Odzak for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when you went with Simo to the command in Pelagicevo, did you go as work obligation to the command or did you go as a soldier to the command in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was my work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So instead of being there as a soldier, right, you always had work obligation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not always. Only until I went to Odzak the first time, but I still kept the weapon that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the uniform?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since you socialised with Simo, you spent a good deal of time together during the day as you drove him here and there, do you have any personal knowledge about Simo Zaric filing criminal charges against the perpetrators of these crimes that you described to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. He didn't tell me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tutnjevic, do you remember sometime in May, 1992, when an attack was carried out against a bus of soldiers from the 4th Detachment somewhere around Novo Selo, do you remember that in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that event because a colleague of mine had been wounded then. The man who was driving the bus. And the attack was carried out by the soldiers that we called Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This settlement of Novo Selo, it's in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac; right?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the settlement in the territory of Bosanski Samac between Brdnik [phoen], Tisina and Grebnice, those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was that? Just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the beginning -- I think it was the beginning of May. Now was it the end of April or the beginning of May, I don't remember the date but I just know that it was when these events just started.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did the army do something about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object, Your Honour. I've let him ask two or three questions -- I let my learned brother ask a few questions, however, this is outside, I've given him some leniency but this is outside the scope of cross-examination. I never questioned on any of these issues and his re-cross or re-direct or whatever it is is outside the scope of my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, let me explain you, all these events are within the scope of the examination [sic] of Prosecution because he asked this witness about Zasavica, and this is what I'm trying to clarify with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This event has nothing to do with Zasavica. It happened elsewhere and it wasn't raised in cross-examination. Can you proceed with other questions, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me explain you. It was raised, Zasavica was raised and we think, the Defence is of the opinion, I don't want to suggest to this witness what is our position so allow me please to ask only one question with regard to this event in Zasavica and you will see what is the relevance. I don't want to suggest anything to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If it's one more question I won't object if he can somehow tie this up to some relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But if it's not relevant I will be objecting again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just answer this, when this happened?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you were saying, could you start again?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When this happened in Novo Selo, this attack against the Serb soldiers and the Serb bus, did the army take some measures in terms of bringing into custody the suspects who were suspected of having attacked this Serb bus? Just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This bus took a shift of soldiers to the line and the army did not bring them into custody because the army never took anybody into custody or into isolation or whatever to the SUP, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. But did the army take any measures after that? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you spoke to the Prosecutor about a number of people who were detained at the SUP, the TO, and so on. Do you know for sure what the grounds were for the arrest of these persons? Do you personally know? You mentioned Tihic, Izetbegovic, et cetera, but do you personally know for sure what the grounds were for their detention?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the basis of your own knowledge, because you were not at the school, at the secondary school or the elementary school but you were at the SUP and the TO that's what you said to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of these two detention centres, who guarded them?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were guarded by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of your knowledge, who was in charge of these two facilities, these two detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the chief of police was Mr. Stevan Todorovic, and then the commander of the police for a while was Milan Jekic from Batkusa, and for a while it was Mr. Savo Cancarevic and now, who was in charge is something I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you specifically. For these detention facilities, was it the army or the police that was in charge of them or some other institution, a third institution?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was exclusively under the jurisdiction of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were asked a whole series of questions by the Prosecutor as to how you as a Yugoslav by conviction viewed certain things. However when I go back through the transcript you said you were a Serb, an ethnic Serb, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My friend just notified me, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well, you are a Serb by ethnicity, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as a Serb, in Samac, back in 1992, before the war broke out, did you feel safe in view of the surroundings of Samac and everything that was happening there? How did you feel?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't feel safe. Because people were divided along ethnic lines, there were attacks being carried out. You were not as free to move about as you used to be before the outbreak of the conflict. That is before the national parties were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you have any information in the spring of 1992 about the existence of the Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understood your question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You personally, did you have any information regarding the existence of a Republic of the Serbian people within Bosnia and Herzegovina, between January and April, 1992? You as a person, did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know exactly what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Republika Srpska in existence then?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure when Republika Srpska was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the existence of the Serbian Municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did. I think there was a public announcement once. It's just that I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was that in the period between January and April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At local level, did the SDS ever publish any announcements concerning the expulsion of non-Serbs or hatred against non-Serbs? Did you ever hear anything like that in Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't and no I didn't hear any such thing from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Finally, can you tell me, if you know the name of any of the perpetrators of the crime in Crkvina? Was this something people talked about?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only name that has ever been dropped is the name of Lugar, Lugar, I know, was a member of that group of volunteers, who had arrived from Serbia, but aside from him, I heard no other names being mentioned. I heard that Josip Orsolic was the first man who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, just one small correction for the transcript, the witness when he was referring to Lugar said the policeman that came from Serbia, and I don't see this in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps the witness can go over the -- can he repeat his answer slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the perpetrators of the crime in Crkvina, the only name that was ever mentioned was the name of Lugar who was a member of the volunteers who had arrived from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I finished with the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one final question from me. You told my colleagues from the Prosecution today when asked about Simo Zaric working on security-related issues in Odzak, you do remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The work obligation that is the arrival of people from Samac municipality to work in Odzak, did that have anything to do with security-related issues?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Security-related issues, do they have anything to do with assigning workers to different tasks, workers who come under work obligation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no link between these two whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tutnjevic. We have finished receiving your evidence. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we bring in the next witness, I would just like for some guidelines in respect to this witness and the following three witnesses after this one who is about to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We were of course advised by the Trial Chamber that we need to stick to these summaries that we provided the Trial Chamber. This is one of the witnesses that was supposed to give his testimony under 71 bis and also the time frames and I really intend to follow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But about this, is there any limitation as for cross-examination of these witnesses? Because if we are about to lead one witness from examination-in-chief for 30 minutes, then I really don't feel it would be fair for the Prosecution to allow them to go for one hour or two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. They will also be restricted within these timeframes because these witnesses were supposed to be on depositions. There reason the Trial Chamber moved them to come to The Hague was because the Trial Chamber wanted to observe them. That was the only reason. So they will stick to the time limits and the incidents that they are supposed to discuss. The Prosecution's cross-examination will also be limited to mostly because these are 40, 40, to half the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand that it's one half of 40 minutes or, for example, if I lead the witness for 40 minutes, they are allowed to 20 minutes? Or?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just needed to have some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In fact, most of these witnesses are discussing matters which have already been discussed by several witnesses so there is nothing knew. Mr. Lukic? I think I saw Mr. Lukic first, before Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I merely wanted to inform the Trial Chamber, in view of the time limits given for these witnesses, that my witnesses, that's Mr. Tadic's 92 bis Rule witnesses can start testifying on Monday. That's what I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber about, as I said they would be ready on the 31st. I took important steps for three of them who didn't even have valid passports to have new passports issued to them, and they will be here on Monday. That's the only thing I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber about, concerning the schedule for Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are -- the Trial Chamber is aware that your witnesses can only start on Monday and they will all come so that we finish, we complete them at one go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I think we'll follow your schedule exactly, in one go, in a quick succession, I think we can deal with it quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that we finalise Mr. Tadic's witnesses. Yes, thank you. Oh, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to Your Honour's ruling and specifically in relation to the next witness I understand, waiting outside, Mr. Naser Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it Mr. Naser Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We were told at 6.00 last night that the next witness was Naser Sejdic so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not Savo? I see. Okay. It will be Mr. Naser Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It will be Mr. Naser Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Firstly we are having great difficulty in working out the order of witnesses, we were advised last night about 6.00 that the next witness was Mr. Sejdic, we had -- no searches had been done we have done some emergency searches to try and find out who this person is and what he was to testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because the filings had been done sometime back, if you look at the joint Defence filings for which were done in November actually, that's where the summaries are for most of these --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a very tiny summary for this particular witness. What we need is the order of witnesses so we can prepare ourselves one after another because we have three people here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe I can ask Mr. Lazarevic or Mr. Pisarevic since they are all here so they can tell us how they intend to call them. The first one as you say will Naser Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will explain that. This is to be honest and I believe that my colleagues know that very well, it would be the fifth time that I'm giving this same information but let me do it again. As soon as we learned that Mr. Naser Sejdic has some problems home and it was when he arrived and it was last week, we informed the Registry and of course the Prosecution that instead of Mr. Petric Andrija, he will come to testify first. Among these four witnesses that are supposed to give their statements under Rule 71. So that was the change that was made because he really had some problems home and he needs to go back home as soon as possible. So after that, two of our witnesses due to some problems of accommodation here in The Hague were transferred to Leiden and they are now in Leiden so we really had a lot of problems about organising all these but finally, at the end of the last week we informed the Registry and of course our colleagues from the Prosecution about the order of the remaining four witnesses. So Mr. Naser Sejdic is the first one who will testify. After him it will be Mr. Petric Andrija. After Mr. Petric Andrija, it's Savo Djurdjevic. And finally, it would be Mr. Goran Buzakovic and that's the definite order because as I explained we had a lot of problems in accommodation with witnesses with their particular demands and everything but I believe by now I also informed the Prosecution on many occasions about all these changes that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, can we have the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hadn't finished. Something I have to say in relation to the next witness which I was -- which I was alluding to before the Court officer brings the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe the usher can just stand by the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness, Mr. Sejdic, he is a witness about whom a number of references or about which five, four our five witnesses have testified as to his involvement as to what happened after the takeover in Bosanski Samac. The witnesses were Witness C, Witness M, Jelena Kapetanovic and Kemal and Ediba Bobic, all gave evidence of this person basically doing house to house searches in company with the 4th Detachment as a police officer, and taking them back to the police station or some of them back where they were beaten severely by Mr. Todorovic. The witness is really in the -- is possibly in the category of an uncharged co-accused, given what must have been his knowledge and the extensive evidence given before the Trial Chamber so far as to what was occurring in the police station in April and May, 1992. If the witness who is working there and the evidence was unchallenged during the Prosecution case says that he was unaware of what was happening, his evidence would have to be incapable of belief given the quantity the sheer volume of evidence about what was occurring at the police station. Having said that, his role, which is so far been revealed in the transcript unchallenged by the Defence, of his role in searching for weapons and arresting people, and he must have had the knowledge of the system of persecution which was then in place, would at least place him in the category of someone who was aiding and abetting, if not committing acts in furtherance of what the Prosecution says is a common purpose. For that reason, the reason of the evidence which is already on the transcript before these proceedings as to his role, the Prosecution submits that the witness should be warned under Rule 90(E) that he is not -- he should not be compelled to incriminate himself, although he may of course -- can be compelled to give the answer. Now, having said that, I note Your Honours's ruling in relation to cross-examination limits. Rule 90(H) of course, 90(H)(i) says that cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter, the evidence in chief, matters affecting the credibility of the witness, and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, here the Prosecution, the subject matter of that case. Clearly, from what the witness clearly from the evidence given about this witness's actions to date in this case, and I can give Your Honours the transcript references if you wish to go back and look at them, this witness can give highly relevant evidence as to what exactly was occurring in the police station, who was arranging it, his role, which are matters which are highly relevant to the Trial Chamber's determination and to the party cross-examining him, that is the Prosecution. Now of course in the 20 minutes or 40 minutes whichever it is or half an hour we just simply can't even start to get into that especially when there are numerous objections and clarifications to the transcript which eat into an already-limited amount of time for cross-examination. Now, this witness in my submission is one who is -- whose evidence, whose cross-examination should not be that constricted because there are highly relevant matters we would wish to put to him including of course his own participation in the system so those are my submissions in relation to what the Prosecution said should happen to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that I need to have -- I need to answer just very briefly to what my colleague has just said. Our next witness was a member of Serbian police but he's not the first member of Serbian police who testified here before this Tribunal, and this issue suddenly raises with this witness, although we had a police officer of highest -- higher rank who testified before this Tribunal and the Prosecution didn't have a problem with all -- with him giving his testimony about that. If there is anything that we should know about the witness, I believe that the Prosecution should have informed us earlier. They have the data of this witness, they have a name of this witness, the summary of this witness, for months, and I don't believe it's fair to raise this question right this moment. After then again, in 40 minutes, and I promise that to the Prosecution, because I informed them about what this witness will testify about, he will -- he will give evidence also on incidents he was involved, and that were mentioned before this Tribunal by other witnesses here. And I believe that he can give his explanation, he was -- I mean, I don't want to say anything before he really starts to giving his testimony. I don't want to make any prejudice here, but this is not the witness who is avoiding these topics. So I believe that this submission of the Prosecution has just made is not established.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I briefly respond for Your Honour's benefit and for my learned friends? I referred to evidence which is before this Trial Chamber. I can give you the names of the witnesses and the transcript references so everyone can look at it for themselves. There is no secret about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. I'm very much aware of what the evidence is, which is on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But the point is, these are witnesses which we moved from the deposition to come before the Trial Chamber so that we can observe them. That is one point. The second point is that the Prosecution has had sufficient opportunity to cross-examine on all the matters that went on in the police station with the other witnesses. Besides their own -- their own witness in the Prosecution case. So the Trial Chamber does not believe that you need any more time than what is -- you are limited to now because the Trial Chamber is not interested in repeating the same issues that have been discussed before with the other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not -- I was not proposing in any way to take the witness to events which are so established or unchallenged that is what happened in the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we proceed, Mr. Re? Please sit down. We have discussed enough about these witnesses and the nature of the evidence they are going to give so you just deal with the witness within the time that the Trial Chamber will give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My point was about the warning to the witness because there are matters there on the transcript which could incriminate him if I ask him certain questions or he gives evidence. That was my primary submission that he could incriminate himself in relation to matters which are in evidence and which I was pointing to. That was my primary concern for this witness. The cross-examination time limit is a secondary one. That's why I wanted to take you to the -- inform you of the transcript page references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It appears to me that perhaps the Trial Chamber would like to look at the relevant provisions. So maybe we will start with this witness tomorrow, since we have only a few minutes before the end of our session. So we will rise and continue with our proceedings tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 1.42 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of March, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25
